## Introduction

In an era of digital streaming versus physical media, prediction for artist success within the music industry can be challenging.

Using the CRISP-DM methodology and tidyverse R packages, we will be exploring a data set from Rolling Stones: 500 Greatest Albums of All Time. Here, we will walk through the methods used to ascertain patterns related to music rankings.

## Background

Beginning in 2003, the Rolling Stones magazine lists an editorial ranking for the albums deemed most significant within the world of music. Whilst Rolling Stones have updated their canon to include current artists on streaming platforms such as Spotify, artists do often remove their discography from streaming services for various reasons; more recently in 18 September 2025, Massive Attack announced their boycott of Spotify under 'No Music for Genocide'. Another challenge which affects music data and may impact popularity is licensing changes; where the availability of albums to users i.e MBV, Taylor Swift may be altogether restricted or, in some cases, only available in certain countries.

## Business Understanding

The purpose is to describe how the lists’ composition changed. These rankings do not directly measure album sales or represent everyone’s musical preferences, yet it may be of use for those within the realm of marketing to identify a strategy to target online audiences to raise artist interest and boost success.

### Objective

Understand the relationship between album ranking and Spotify streams, so that artists and record companies can make informed decisions to maintain commercial performance. The following questions will be considered:

1.  How is Spotify popularity associated with an album’s position in Rolling Stone 3 year rankings?

2.  Can an album’s release year, genre and historical Billboard performance predict its Spotify popularity?

## Data Understanding & Initial Exploration

We started by loading a raw data set containing various artist metrics. The data set includes objects such as name, year of release, type of album, genre, rank (based on year ranked) and Spotify popularity.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)

# importing my data
rolling_raw <- read_csv(
  "rolling_stone.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

We want to understand what each data type is before changing any behaviors; release year appears as <dbl> -\> does not need converting as years are whole numbers.

```{r}
#| echo: false
head(rolling_raw)
glimpse(rolling_raw)
#check to identify if csv file contained bits R can't read on import
problems(rolling_raw)
```

### Counting rows and columns - how many albums do we begin with?

```{r}
nrow(rolling_raw)
ncol(rolling_raw)
```

## Consideration 1: Missing values

Here we encounter a lot of missing values; 191 missing ranks for years 2003-2020, missing spotify information are key. Reasons for this include older albums tending towards missing a rank, or that artists have removed their work. We should stand on the side of caution to avoid selection bias.The missing Spotify and genre values do not prevent this analysis because our question does not use those variables. Also, a missing Spotify score alone cannot tell us why it is missing

```{r}
#| echo: false
#empty column inspection
colSums(is.na(rolling_raw))
rolling_raw |>
  select(release_year, rank_2003, rank_2012, rank_2020) |>
  is.na() |>
  colSums()
```

## Data Preparation Account for duplicates, excluding however albums by same artist or Na's.

```{r}
#| echo: false
sum(duplicated(rolling_raw))
rolling_unique <- rolling_raw |>
  distinct()

nrow(rolling_raw) - nrow(rolling_unique)

#how many records remain after removing exact duplicates.
nrow(rolling_unique)
```

### Selecting- Keeping release year and ranks

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| # I want album identifiers, release year and rankings retained for decade comparisons.
# Select() use preserves all rows, including values w missing ranks.
rolling_selected <- rolling_unique |>
  select(
    clean_name,
    album,
    release_year,
    rank_2003,
    rank_2012,
    rank_2020
  )

# Have we kept all album records and selected six columns.
dim(rolling_selected)

# See first six records to check columns.
head(rolling_selected)
```

## Ranking Values

A recorded rank must fall between 1 and 500. Filter() to inspect anything outside that range

```{r}
# !na - treating as a valid rank
notvalid_ranks <- rolling_selected |>
  filter(
    (!is.na(rank_2003) & (rank_2003 < 1 | rank_2003 > 500)) |
    (!is.na(rank_2012) & (rank_2012 < 1 | rank_2012 > 500)) |
    (!is.na(rank_2020) & (rank_2020 < 1 | rank_2020 > 500))
  )

# Display any records needing investigation before we change their values.
notvalid_ranks

# Count how many records contain an out-of-range rank.
nrow(notvalid_ranks)
```

## Checking ranking editions 
Having checked ranks 2003-2020, 4 rows have a shared ranking; different artists and albums. These ranks have been left unchanged since no adequate replacements have been located

```{r}
#which ranking numbers appear more than once
#rank 2003
#| echo: false
rolling_selected |>
  filter(!is.na(rank_2003)) |>
  count(rank_2003) |>
  filter(n > 1)
#rank 2012
rolling_selected |>
  filter(!is.na(rank_2012)) |>
  count(rank_2012) |>
  filter(n > 1)
#2020's turn
rolling_selected |>
  filter(!is.na(rank_2020)) |>
  count(rank_2020) |>
  filter(n > 1)

#so only rank 2003- let's find those albums
# Show the albums with either repeated 2003 rank so we can inspect them.
rolling_selected |>
  filter(rank_2003 == 314 | rank_2003 == 493)
#See below- different albums hence not duplicates
```

## Release Decade Column; we wish to make comparisons keeping album rows - using a vectorized function, we use Mutate(). The calculation (release_year / 10) * 10 groups allows for a comparison of both individual years and decades without loop

```{r}
#| echo: false
#  group albums into ten-year periods.
# Divide each release year by 10
# Multiply by 10 to obtain the decade's starting year.
rolling_clean <- rolling_selected |>
  mutate(
    release_decade = (release_year %/% 10) * 10
  )
# Release years vs decades shown
rolling_clean |>
  select(clean_name, album, release_year, release_decade) |>
  head(10)

# Check that  we now have seven columns.
dim(rolling_clean)
```

Grouping by release date:

```{r}
#calculating counts for release decade....
decade_summary <- rolling_clean |>
  group_by(release_decade) |>
  summarise(
    # Count non-missing ranks without changing the original album data.
    albums_2003 = sum(!is.na(rank_2003)),
    albums_2012 = sum(!is.na(rank_2012)),
    albums_2020 = sum(!is.na(rank_2020)),

    # Remove grouping from the completed summary.
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# ordering
decade_summary <- decade_summary |>
  arrange(release_decade)

# inspect counts
decade_summary

#peace of mind check- must add up to 500 so that ranks have been kept
# Add the decade counts to check that each edition has 500 recorded entries.
# This checks our summary without changing the album data.
decade_summary |>
  summarise(
    total_2003 = sum(albums_2003),
    total_2012 = sum(albums_2012),
    total_2020 = sum(albums_2020)
  )
#As one would expect, with time older albums become less popular/rank goes down with time- more modern releases seen to be more influential?

#1950- are all ~10-11 albums the same or what variation do we see
```

Preparing artist location data
```{r}

# Keep one row per artist because location information belongs to the artist.
# This prevents us from researching the same artist separately for every album.
artist_list <- rolling_clean |>
  distinct(clean_name) |>
  arrange(clean_name)

# Count how many artists need location information.
nrow(artist_list)

# Inspect the first ten names before sourcing their locations.
head(artist_list, 10)

```

## Preparing our Location Table

```{r}
# Start with one row per artist to avoid multiplying album rows during the join.
artist_locations <- artist_list |>
  mutate(
    # Create text columns for verified country and city/town information.
    # NA_character_ means a missing text value, not a guessed location.
    country = NA_character_,
    region = NA_character_,

    # Record whether the location describes birthplace or band formation.
    location_basis = NA_character_,

    # Keep a source link so each location can be checked.
    source = NA_character_
  )

# Check that the table has 386 artists and five columns.
dim(artist_locations)

# Inspect the structure before adding verified location information.
head(artist_locations, 10)

```

```{r}
# I missed out genre column so must amend

rolling_selected <- rolling_unique |>
  select(
    clean_name,
    album,
    release_year,
    genre,
    rank_2003,
    rank_2012,
    rank_2020
  )

# Rebuild the prepared data with genre included and release decade added.
rolling_clean <- rolling_selected |>
  mutate(
    release_decade = (release_year %/% 10) * 10
  )

# Check the dimensions and number of missing genre values.
dim(rolling_clean)
sum(is.na(rolling_clean$genre))
```

##Preparing release years and genres for plotting

```{r}
# Keep genre and release year alongside each recorded rank.
rolling_hist_data <- rolling_clean |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(rank_2003, rank_2012, rank_2020),
    names_to = "edition",
    names_prefix = "rank_",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  # Include an album in an edition's histogram only when its rank is recorded.
  # This creates a plotting subset; rolling_clean keeps all original NA values.
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  mutate(
    # Label missing genres so these albums remain visible in the chart.
    # This label does not guess the missing genre.
    genre_display = if_else(
      is.na(genre),
      "Genre not recorded",
      genre
    )
  )

# Check that each edition contributes 500 albums.
rolling_hist_data |>
  count(edition)

# Inspecting the genre labels .
rolling_hist_data |>
  distinct(genre_display) |>
  arrange(genre_display)
```
## ggplot time!!

```{r}
#just check first it's installed
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
#remember x3 things required 
base_plot <- ggplot(
  data = rolling_hist_data,
  aes(x = release_year)
) +
  # Add labels explaining what the chart will show.
  labs(
    title = "Release decades and genres in Rolling Stone's album lists",
    x = "Album release year",
    y = "Number of albums",
    fill = "Genre"
  )

base_plot
```

## Adding more style
```{r}
histogram_plot <- base_plot +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(fill = genre_display),
    binwidth = 10,
    boundary = 1950,
    closed = "left"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ edition, ncol = 1)
# genre text is too high; amendment
histogram_plot <- histogram_plot +
  labs(
    title = "Release decades and genres\nin Rolling Stone's album lists"
  )
histogram_plot
```
